surface.surface-portrait.description: The plate the face illustration is printed on, and the ONE surface that does not walk the ramp to the far end in dark. The portrait is dark line-art over light fills (its densest fill is #DDDCDE), so on a stone-900 page it loses its hair and its jacket and leaves a face floating in the dark — measured, not assumed. Kept light in both themes it reads as a printed card lying on the page, which is the same 'object on the sheet' language as the nav bar's drop shadow, and it avoids the alternative everyone reaches for first: a CSS invert() filter, which makes an uncanny negative of a human face and flips his blue collar to orange. It is stone-100 rather than stone-50 in dark because at 3.5rem on near-black the brightest paper in the ramp is a light source rather than a card; stone-100 is the page's own light-theme paper, which is exactly the fiction being maintained. No print value: the drawer that carries it is display:none on paper.

chrome.chrome-label-on-strong.description: Text sitting on chrome-bg-strong (the footer). Has no dark variant on purpose: that surface is near-black in BOTH themes, so its label must stay light in both. 6.96:1 on slate-900, 7.87:1 on slate-950. It DOES need a print value: on paper that surface turns white, so a light label would vanish.

chrome.chrome-grid.description: The skeleton's square lines — slate-500 at 16% on paper, slate-400 at 14% on dark (a lighter ink at lower alpha, so the grid stays a whisper rather than becoming a cage). Prints as nothing: the grid is screen scaffolding, not content.

accent.accent.description: Prints as ink, not blue. A CV is as likely to be printed greyscale as in colour, and blue reduced to mid-grey reads as a mistake rather than an accent.

accent.accent-rgb.description: rgb triplet of --accent, for rgba() composition in JS and hover states

effect.shadow-drop.description: The hard offset shadow under the floating nav — an object lying on the sheet. Deeper and more opaque in dark, where a 15% veil would vanish. Nothing on paper: a shadow printed is just a grey smear.

effect.scrim.description: The veil behind the case-study dialog. Warm stone in light (it dims paper), cold slate in dark (it dims chrome).

automata.automata-cell-rgb.description: The resident population — stone-500 on paper, stone-400 on dark (the ramp inverts with the surface, or the cells would sink into the page)

text.text-2xs.description: The floor. Chips, the tool trace, the source list's ordinals, the ▪ bullets — text you are not meant to read so much as recognise.

text.text-xs.description: The standard chrome label: the nav bar, buttons, section numbers, dated spans, page notes. Twelve of the old 89 declarations were already this value — it was the de-facto step, now it is the actual one.

text.text-sm.description: Small prose — captions, fact labels, citation lines, code blocks.

text.text-md.description: Secondary prose: card copy, list items, definition bodies. Body's quieter sibling.

text.text-base.description: Body. Set on `body` in components.css; everything else is measured from here.

text.text-lead.description: The reading lede — one step above body, the paragraph that introduces a section. On paper it collapses back into body: a CV has no room for an emphasised opening size.

text.text-sub.description: Sub-titles: card titles, a role in an entry, an <h3> inside a case study. Three near-identical ramps used to live here — clamp(1.15rem,1.7vw,1.45rem), clamp(1.1rem,1.9vw,1.45rem) and clamp(1.2rem,2.2vw,1.55rem) — rendering at 1280px as 21.76 / 23.2 / 24.8px. That is drift, not hierarchy. A fourth, the work index's project name, was a genuine step larger and became `text-heading`.

text.text-heading.description: One step above a sub-title and below a section title: the work index's project names, which are the largest thing in a scannable list and must not fall back to card-title size.

text.text-title.description: Section titles and the one statement per section. `.t-title` and `.t-statement` were 2.9rem and 2.7rem — the same level wearing different weights and cases, which is what the utility classes are for.

text.text-display.description: Display: dialog titles, the CV name, a stat, a fact's number. `.fact__num` was clamp(2.2rem, 4.5vw, 3.5rem) and `.stat` was clamp(2.2rem, 5vw, 3.5rem) — a 0.5vw difference nobody chose.

text.text-display-hero.description: The hero name, once per site.

text.text-code.description: Inline <code> inside prose. A RATIO, not a step: monospace runs optically larger than the sans beside it, so it is set relative to whatever paragraph it lands in.

text.text-unit.description: The unit suffix riding on a display number (`+`, `%`, `×`). A ratio for the same reason: it must stay proportional to the number it annotates, whatever size that number lands at.

space.space-nav.description: Clearance under the fixed nav bar, on every page head. Prints as nothing: `.bar` is display:none on paper, so the clearance would be 88px of blank at the top of the sheet.

border.rule-strong.description: The heavy rule. In light it is drawn ink — the section signature. Inverting it literally would make it a 2px stone-50 bar glaring across every section top, so on dark it becomes the strong chrome border instead: still structural, no longer a light source. On paper it returns to ink — the one place the rule is cheap and does the most work.
